title: RISC-V: Registers, Arithmetic, and Shifts
summary: This unit explores the modular RISC-V ISA (modulare RISC-V-ISA), register conventions (Registerkonventionen), and signed and unsigned arithmetic (signed- und unsigned-Arithmetik). You will learn how multiplication and division (Multiplikation und Division) and shifts (Shifts) change bit patterns, and which pseudoinstructions (Pseudobefehle) and immediate operations (Immediate-Operationen) are used for them. The unit concludes with common errors in assembly programming (Assemblerprogrammierung).
keyFacts: `RV32` denotes a RISC-V variant with 32-bit registers; `I` stands for the integer base, and `M` for multiplication and division.
`RV32I` has 32 registers, from `x0` to `x31`, each 32 bits wide.
`x0` always returns zero; no initial value should be assumed for any other register.
Register names such as `a0`, `s0`, and `t0` are usage conventions and do not indicate different register types.
`mul` returns the low 32 product bits; `mulh`, `mulhu`, and `mulhsu` return high product bits with different signedness interpretations.
`div` and `rem` operate on signed values; `divu` and `remu` operate on unsigned values.
`sll` and `slli` fill the vacated rightmost positions with zeros during a left shift; `srl` and `srli` fill the vacated leftmost positions with zeros during a logical right shift.
`sra` and `srai` fill the vacated leftmost positions with copies of the sign bit during an arithmetic right shift.
A one-bit left shift is reliably equivalent to multiplication by 2 only if the result fits in the chosen word width.
For negative odd numbers, an arithmetic right shift can differ from signed division because division rounds toward zero.
A pseudoinstruction is not a machine instruction of its own; the assembler translates it into real instructions.
`li` may require different numbers of real instructions depending on the constant; for large constants, `lui` and `addi` are examples of instructions that may be used.
An immediate is a constant encoded directly in an instruction.
Sign extension must be taken into account for negative immediates.
When programming in assembly, check register values, signedness, loop behavior, and register assignments step by step.

review.notes: Ein Distraktor in der RV32I-Frage war mehrdeutig, weil Multiplikation und Division als Erweiterung M verstanden werden konnten; er wurde eindeutig als falsche Basiszuordnung formuliert. Alle 42 Fragen wurden geprüft; Rechenwerte, Antwortmengen, Quellenüberschriften und Formalia sind konsistent.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes `RV32I`?

options.text: 32-bit variant whose base includes multiplication and division

questions.explanation: `RV32` denotes 32-bit registers, and `I` stands for the integer base. Multiplication and division are part of the `M` extension.

questions.prompt: Select all correct mappings. More than one answer may be correct.
questions.explanation: `I` denotes the integer base, `M` denotes multiplication and division, and `F` denotes floating-point operations. `A` stands for atomic operations, and `V` for vector operations.

questions.prompt: `RV32I` has 32 registers, from `x0` to `x31`, and each register is 32 bits wide.
questions.explanation: The registers range from `x0` to `x31`, giving 32 registers in total. In `RV32I`, each register is 32 bits wide.

questions.prompt: The register `x0` always returns ___.
questions.explanation: `x0` is the zero register and always returns zero, regardless of other instructions.

questions.prompt: What do names such as `a0`, `s0`, and `t0` mean in RISC-V?

options.text: They are fixed hardware types with different arithmetic capabilities.
They are alternative names for machine instructions.
They are usage conventions for registers.
They denote three different register widths.

questions.explanation: These names describe conventional roles, such as argument, saved, or temporary registers. They are still ordinary registers.

questions.prompt: What information does `mul` provide for 32-bit operands?

options.text: The low 32 bits of the product
The high 32 bits of an unsigned product
The high 32 bits of a signed product

questions.explanation: `mul` returns the low part of the product. The instructions `mulh`, `mulhu`, or `mulhsu` are used to obtain high product bits.

source.heading: Multiplikation und Division: signed oder unsigned?

questions.prompt: Select all correct mappings. More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: `mulhu` returns the low product bits for two unsigned operands.
`mulhsu` interprets the first operand as signed and the second as unsigned.
`mulh` returns high product bits for two signed operands.

questions.explanation: `mulh` uses signed/signed operands, `mulhsu` uses signed/unsigned operands, and `div` and `rem` both operate on signed values. `mulhu` returns high, not low, product bits; `divu` and `remu` are unsigned.

questions.prompt: How does `srl` fill the positions vacated on the left during a right shift?

options.text: With copies of the sign bit

questions.explanation: `srl` is a logical right shift and fills the leftmost positions with zeros. Copying the sign bit is the behavior of `sra`.

questions.prompt: A pseudoinstruction is a machine instruction of its own with a separate opcode.
questions.explanation: A pseudoinstruction is only a readable assembly notation. The assembler translates it into one or more real machine instructions.

questions.prompt: An immediate is a ___ encoded directly in an instruction.
questions.explanation: An immediate is a fixed numeric value encoded in an instruction; it is not read from a register first.

questions.prompt: Which operation keeps only the low four bits when `t0 = 0x2C`?
questions.explanation: `andi` with the mask `0x0F` sets all higher bits to zero and keeps only the low four bits.

questions.prompt: Which extensions are included in `RV32IM`?

options.text: 32-bit registers, the integer base, and multiplication/division
64-bit registers, the integer base, and floating-point operations

questions.explanation: `RV32` indicates the register width, `I` denotes the integer base, and `M` adds multiplication and division.

questions.prompt: The 4-bit patterns `1101` and `0010` are multiplied as signed values. What 8-bit result is produced?
questions.explanation: As signed values, `1101` represents −3 and `0010` represents 2. Their product is −6, represented as `1111 1010`.

source.heading: Multiplikation und Division: signed oder unsigned?

questions.prompt: The 4-bit patterns `0110` and `0101` are multiplied as unsigned numbers. The full product is represented using 8 bits. What bit pattern is produced?
questions.explanation: As unsigned numbers, the operands are 6 and 5. Their product is 30, which is represented by the 8-bit pattern `0001 1110`.

questions.prompt: Which instruction computes a quotient using a signed interpretation?
questions.explanation: `div` returns the signed quotient. `divu` is the unsigned variant; `rem` and `remu` each return the remainder.

questions.prompt: Compute the 8-bit left shift `0010 1100 << 1`.
questions.explanation: A left shift moves the bits one position to the left and appends a 0 on the right. The result is `0101 1000`, which is 88.

questions.prompt: Compute the logical right shift `1101 0000 >> 1`.
questions.explanation: A logical right shift appends a 0 on the left. `1101 0000` becomes `0110 1000`, which represents unsigned 104.

questions.prompt: Compute the arithmetic right shift `1101 0000 >> 1`.
questions.explanation: The sign bit 1 is copied on the left. This produces `1110 1000`, which represents −24 in 8-bit two's complement.

questions.prompt: Which sequence of real instructions can replace `not t0, t1`?
questions.explanation: XOR with a bit mask consisting entirely of ones flips every bit. Therefore, `not` expands to `xori t0, t1, -1`.

questions.prompt: Given `t0 = 0x2C`, what value does `ori t2, t0, 0x10` produce?
questions.explanation: `0x2C` is `0010 1100`, and `0x10` is `0001 0000`. The bitwise OR produces `0011 1100`, or `0x3C`.

questions.prompt: Given `t0 = 0x2C`, what value does `addi t1, t0, 4` produce?
questions.explanation: `0x2C` represents 44. Adding 4 gives 48, or `0x30`.

questions.prompt: A one-bit left shift is reliably equivalent to multiplication by 2 only when the mathematical result fits in the chosen word width.
questions.explanation: The bit operation itself is always the same, but during overflow, bits shifted off the left are lost. The resulting bit pattern then no longer represents the full product.

questions.prompt: Select all correct statements. More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: Names such as `a0` and `t0` are usage conventions.
An initial value of zero may be assumed for every register except `x0`.

questions.explanation: Only `x0` is guaranteed to be zero. No initial value is assumed for other registers; their names describe conventional roles.

questions.prompt: How do you obtain the full 64-bit product of two signed 32-bit operands?

options.text: Low bits with `mul`, high bits with `mulhu`
Low bits with `mulh`, high bits with `mul`
Low bits with `mul`, high bits with `mulh`

questions.explanation: `mul` returns the low part of the product. For two signed operands, `mulh` returns the corresponding high part.

questions.prompt: Consider the 4-bit patterns `1101` and `0011`. Multiply them once as unsigned numbers and once as signed numbers in 4-bit two's complement, and give both full products using 8 bits. Statement: For these operands, the low 4 bits of the products are the same, while the high 4 bits differ. Is the statement true or false?
questions.explanation: As unsigned numbers, the patterns give $13\cdot3=39$, or `0010 0111`. In 4-bit two's complement, they represent $-3$ and $3$; their product $-9$ is represented in 8-bit two's complement as `1111 0111`. Both products end in `0111`, but their high 4 bits are `0010` and `1111`.

questions.prompt: To divide negative odd signed values by 2 correctly, use ___ instead of an arithmetic right shift.
questions.explanation: For negative odd numbers, an arithmetic right shift can round down. `div` performs signed division with rounding toward zero.

questions.prompt: `1101 0001` represents the signed value −47. Which combination of shift and division by 2 is correct?
questions.explanation: The arithmetic shift produces `1110 1000`, or −24. Signed division of −47 by 2 rounds toward zero and gives −23.

questions.prompt: Select all correct statements about shift instructions. More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: `sra` fills the leftmost positions with copies of the sign bit.
The suffix `i` marks the immediate variant.
The shift amount can be specified in a register or directly in the instruction.
`srl` fills the leftmost positions with copies of the sign bit.

questions.explanation: The variants without `i` use a register, while those with `i` use an immediate. `sra` preserves the sign, whereas `srl` inserts zeros on the left.

questions.prompt: Which statement about `li` is correct?

options.text: `li` can load only the value zero.
`li` always expands to exactly one machine instruction.
`li` is a real instruction in the M extension.
`li` may require multiple real instructions, depending on the constant.

questions.explanation: For small constants, a single `addi` is often sufficient; larger constants can be constructed using, for example, `lui` and `addi`. Therefore, there is no fixed expansion for every `li`.

questions.prompt: For negative immediates, I need to account for ___.
questions.explanation: A negative immediate is sign-extended to the register width. This preserves its signed meaning and the correct upper bits.

questions.prompt: At the start of an assembly program, all registers except `x0` may be assumed to be zero.
questions.explanation: Only `x0` is guaranteed to return zero. The initial value of any other register is unknown unless it was initialized beforehand.

questions.prompt: Which check directly helps prevent loops from running one iteration too many or too few?

options.text: Check the start, termination condition, and number of iterations

questions.explanation: The loop length depends on the starting state, the termination condition, and the actual number of iterations. The other checks do not directly address this issue.

questions.prompt: Select all useful practices when programming in assembly. More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: Plan the execution flow and register assignments before writing the code.
Always treat uninitialized registers as zero.
Trace the program instruction by instruction and check register values.

questions.explanation: Planning, comments, and step-by-step checking make the code easier to follow and help with debugging. Uninitialized registers, however, must not automatically be treated as zero.

questions.prompt: An assembly program uses the pseudoinstruction `neg`. Which statement correctly describes the relationship between the ISA and the pseudoinstruction?

options.text: The ISA describes only register conventions, not machine instructions.
`neg` automatically adds a new opcode to the hardware.
Pseudoinstructions belong only to the operating-system layer and are not translated.
The ISA defines real machine instructions; the assembler replaces `neg` with those instructions.

questions.explanation: The ISA defines the executable machine instructions. `neg` is only a readable notation and is expanded, for example, into `sub t0, x0, t1`.

questions.prompt: What bit sequence is in a 32-bit register after `addi t0, x0, -1`?
questions.explanation: `x0` returns zero. The negative immediate is sign-extended, so −1 is represented in 32 bits as `0xFFFFFFFF`.

questions.prompt: For `ld a1, 8(s0)`, the effective address is ...
questions.explanation: For a load, `a1` is the destination register. The memory address is formed from the base register `s0` and the offset 8.

questions.prompt: An 8-bit pattern `1101 0000` is shifted one position to the right. Select all correct statements. More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: Both instructions produce the same bit pattern.
`srai` fills the leftmost positions with zeros.

questions.explanation: `srli` inserts a 0 on the left, while `srai` copies the sign bit 1. The resulting bit patterns and interpretations therefore differ.

questions.explanation: As unsigned numbers, the product is 13 · 2 = 26, or `0001 1010`. As signed numbers, the product is −3 · 2 = −6, or `1111 1010`.

questions.prompt: The full product requires the high bits; the first operand is signed and the second is unsigned. Which instruction returns the high part of the product?
questions.explanation: `mulhsu` is specifically for a signed first operand and an unsigned second operand. Regardless of signedness, `mul` returns only the low product bits.

questions.prompt: Which sequence of real instructions implements the pseudoinstruction `neg t0, t1`?
questions.explanation: Because `x0` always returns zero, `sub t0, x0, t1` computes 0 − `t1`, producing the negated value.

questions.prompt:
Given `t0 = 0x2C`, execute the three instructions; each reads the unchanged value from `t0` and writes to its own destination register:

- `ori t1, t0, 0x10`
- `xori t2, t0, 0x0F`
- `andi t3, t0, 0x0F`

Which result line is completely correct? Results are given in hexadecimal.
questions.explanation: `0x2C OR 0x10 = 0x3C`, `0x2C XOR 0x0F = 0x23`, and `0x2C AND 0x0F = 0x0C`. All three instructions read the given value from `t0`.

questions.prompt: When checking an assembly program, select all correct practices. More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: Before doing a calculation, determine whether the interpretation is signed or unsigned.
You may assume `t0` and `t1` are zero without initializing them.
For loops, check the start, termination condition, and number of iterations.
After each relevant instruction, check the values of the affected registers.

questions.explanation: Signedness, register values, and loop conditions are common sources of errors. Only `x0` is automatically zero; `t0` and `t1` are not.

questions.prompt: The 8-bit pattern `1101 0000` is shifted one position to the left. Which statement correctly describes the result?

options.text: The pattern is `1010 0000`; it represents signed −96 and unsigned 160.
The pattern is `1010 0000`; it represents 416 as both signed and unsigned.
The pattern is `0110 1000`; it represents unsigned 104.
The pattern is `1110 1000`; it represents signed −24.

questions.explanation: The bit shift produces `1010 0000`. This pattern can be interpreted as signed −96 or unsigned 160; the full unsigned product 208 · 2 = 416 does not fit in 8 bits.

questions.prompt: If an unsigned left shift of `1101 0000` produces the bit pattern `1010 0000`, which represents 160, no overflow has occurred.
questions.explanation: The bit pattern does represent 160 within 8 bits, but the full product is 208 · 2 = 416, which does not fit in 8 bits. The leftmost bit, along with other product bits, was lost.

levels.title: In Practice: Bits, Numbers, and Real Systems

questions.prompt: Your smartwatch packs eight yes/no states into one byte. Which operations are typical tools for working with this kind of bit field?

options.text: Use `OR` to set a flag without clearing other set bits
Use `div` to isolate any flag directly
Use `AND` to read a single status flag

questions.explanation: Bitwise logical operations are ideal for compact status fields: `AND` masks, `OR` sets, and `XOR` toggles individual bits. You will encounter these patterns in devices, protocols, and drivers.

questions.prompt: In a game, a score is stored as an 8-bit unsigned value. You want to double it with a one-bit left shift. When is this guaranteed to be a true doubling?

options.text: Only if an arithmetic right shift follows it
Always, because shifting cannot cause overflow
Only if the most significant bit was 1 beforehand
Only if the mathematical result fits in 8 bits

questions.explanation: A left shift appends zeros on the right, but discards bits that fall off the left. Therefore, it is guaranteed to be equivalent to multiplication by 2 only when the result fits in the word width.

source.heading: Links um eine Stelle: Multiplikation mit 2

questions.prompt: A sensor protocol reserves 12 bits for a measurement. How many different bit patterns can this field represent?
questions.explanation: Each of the 12 bits can be 0 or 1, so there are 2^12 = 4096 different bit patterns.

questions.prompt: A temperature sensor returns the signed value −47. Your code must divide it by 2 as an integer and round toward zero. Which RISC-V tool is appropriate?
questions.explanation: The signed instruction `div` from the M extension rounds −47 divided by 2 toward zero and returns −23. An arithmetic right shift instead gives −24 because it rounds down for negative values.

questions.prompt: When assembling, `li t0, 100000` is used, and you want to estimate how many instructions your program actually executes. Which statement is realistic?

options.text: `li` is a pseudoinstruction and may expand into several real instructions depending on the constant
`li` is always exactly one machine instruction

questions.explanation: `li` is only a readable shorthand. For larger constants, the assembler may generate `lui` and `addi`, for example, so the expansion depends on the specific number.

questions.prompt: An 8-bit game counter contains the unsigned value 208. What value remains in the 8-bit register after a one-bit left shift?
questions.explanation: 208 is the bit pattern 11010000. After `<< 1`, the result is 10100000, or 160. The mathematical product 416 does not fit in 8 bits, so the leftmost bit is discarded.

questions.prompt: Is this correct? In a network packet, the low four bits of a status field are flags. `andi` with the mask `0x0F` can isolate these four bits without including the upper bits in the result.
questions.explanation: A bitwise AND with `0x0F` preserves only the low four bits; all other result bits become zero. This is a typical use of immediate masks.

questions.prompt: How many different 32-bit patterns can a writable data register in RV32 store?
questions.explanation: A writable RV32 data register has 32 bits. Each bit can be 0 or 1, so there are 2^32 = 4,294,967,296 different bit patterns. The register `x0`, which is hardwired to zero, is not meant here.

questions.prompt: You are reading a RISC-V function from a library: one result is returned in `a0`, while `s0` must be preserved across a function call. What explains this?

options.text: The two names automatically trigger multiplication by 2
`a0` and `s0` are hardware register types that differ from `x0` through `x31`
Every register starts automatically with the value zero
Register conventions for arguments, return values, and saved registers

questions.explanation: `a0` and `s0` are alternative names for registers with agreed roles. These conventions help compilers, libraries, and subroutines work together, but they do not change the register hardware.

questions.prompt: A big-integer library, such as one used in cryptography, multiplies two unsigned 32-bit limbs and needs the full 64-bit product. Which statements apply?

options.text: `mulh` is always correct because signedness does not matter for the high bits
`mulhu` returns the high 32 product bits for two unsigned operands
`mul` alone is always sufficient because multiplying two 32-bit numbers produces at most 32 product bits

questions.explanation: To obtain the full product, combine the low bits from `mul` with the appropriate high bits. For unsigned limbs, `mulhu` from the M extension provides the high bits; signedness therefore matters.
